texts.FRA:
France welcomes Germany's resolution2467 (2019) as a milestone, not the end of our effort. Its survivor-centred approach, strengthened Patten mandate and requested Secretary-General report on children born of rape by2021 are advances. The report is requested, not completed.

We condemn the health-language omission under permanent-member pressure and veto threats. Victims need sexual and reproductive health care; the omission undermines dignity. Women freely decide about their bodies, including terminating involuntary pregnancies. We will continue promoting full care and rights in every context, in the Council, other UN bodies and elsewhere. Reaffirmed provisions—2106 paragraph19 and1889 paragraph10—remain part of our framework despite the omission.

For this hypothetical exercise, I recommend revising P: provide immediate comprehensive sexual/reproductive care without a conviction gate, using funded survivor-referral services and a separate voluntary protected referral route for investigation and prosecution. Parallel care and accountability require staffing, funding and coordination, but awaiting conviction harms access. These analytical recommendations are not an observed French endorsement of P or a future vote. Our real ongoing care commitments remain established.
texts.GBR:
The United Kingdom welcomes Germany's achievement in adopting resolution2467 (2019), while regretting omitted language on comprehensive sexual and reproductive services. The survivor-centred approach recognizes conflict-related sexual violence's disproportionate impact on women and girls and civil society's important role. Further work on justice and accountability remains necessary.

Access to comprehensive sexual and reproductive health care is essential to a genuine survivor-centred approach. Our continuing worldwide support for survivors' access remains a real commitment.

For this hypothetical exercise, I recommend revising P to remove the final-conviction gate and restore immediate comprehensive care. Fund survivor-referral services for care alongside a separate voluntary protected evidence-referral route for investigation and prosecution. Staffing, funding and coordination must sustain both tracks; waiting for convictions instead harms timely care. These are analytical operational recommendations, not an observed UK endorsement of P or a guaranteed future vote. Earlier adoption and continuing care support do not establish those unknown decisions.
